title: Metabolism of Hexoses Other Than Glucose
objectives: Understand the metabolic pathways of fructose, galactose, and mannose
Compare hepatic vs. extrahepatic fructose metabolism
Explain clinical consequences of hexose metabolism disorders
Describe the relationship between fructose intake and metabolic syndrome

fructose.title: Fructose Metabolism
fructose.content:
Fructose Metabolic Pathways

Fructose is metabolized through distinct pathways in liver (fructose-1-P pathway) and extrahepatic tissues (direct phosphorylation to fructose-6-P).

Hepatic Pathway

1. Fructokinase

Reaction: Fructose → Fructose-1-P (liver-specific)

Significance: Bypasses PFK-1 regulation

2. Aldolase B

Reaction: Cleaves Fructose-1-P → DHAP + Glyceraldehyde

Tissue: Liver-specific isozyme

Extrahepatic Pathway

Hexokinase

Reaction: Fructose → Fructose-6-P (enters glycolysis)

Tissues: Muscle, adipose, kidney, intestine

fructose_clinical.title: Fructose Disorders
fructose_clinical.content:
Clinical Aspects of Fructose Metabolism

Essential Fructosuria

Cause: Fructokinase deficiency

Features: Benign, asymptomatic fructosuria

Management: Low fructose/sucrose/sorbitol diet

Hereditary Fructose Intolerance

Cause: Aldolase B deficiency

Symptoms:

  • Severe hypoglycemia after fructose intake
  • Vomiting, liver dysfunction
  • Pi sequestration → ATP depletion

High Fructose Consequences

Metabolic: Hypertriglyceridemia (excess acetyl-CoA → VLDL)

Gout: Fructose-1-P inhibits purine degradation → hyperuricemia

Diabetic Complications: Sorbitol accumulation → cataracts/neuropathy

galactose.title: Galactose Metabolism
galactose.content:
Galactose-1-P Pathway

1. Galactokinase

Reaction: Galactose → Galactose-1-P

2. Galactose-1-P Uridyltransferase

Reaction: Galactose-1-P + UDP-glucose → UDP-galactose + Glucose-1-P

Key Step: Produces glycolytic intermediate

3. UDP-Galactose Epimerase

Reaction: Converts UDP-galactose ↔ UDP-glucose (NAD-dependent)

Functions: Lactose synthesis (mammary), glycoprotein/glycolipid production

galactose_clinical.title: Galactosemia
galactose_clinical.content:
Galactosemia Types

Type 1 (Classic)

Defect: Galactose-1-P uridyltransferase (GALT)

Consequences:

  • Galactose-1-P accumulation → Pi depletion
  • Liver failure, mental retardation, cataracts
  • Even dietary restriction doesn't prevent complications

Type 2

Defect: Galactokinase deficiency

Main Symptom: Cataracts from galactitol accumulation

Treatment: Dietary galactose restriction effective

Type 3

Defect: UDP-galactose-4-epimerase (GALE)

Note: Milder symptoms if transferase intact

mannose.title: Mannose Metabolism
mannose.content:
Mannose Pathways

Phosphomannose Isomerase

Reaction: Mannose-6-P ↔ Fructose-6-P

Glycolytic Entry: Connects to glycolysis intermediates

Biosynthetic Roles

Glycoprotein synthesis: Mannose incorporated into N-linked oligosaccharides

Lysosomal enzymes: Mannose-6-P targets enzymes to lysosomes

faqs.title: FAQs
faqs.content:
Frequently Asked Questions

Why does fructose metabolism cause hyperuricemia?
Fructose-1-P sequesters Pi → ATP depletion → reduced inhibition of purine degradation → increased uric acid production.
How does classic galactosemia differ from type 2?
Type 1 (GALT) causes systemic toxicity from galactose-1-P accumulation, while type 2 (galactokinase) mainly causes cataracts via galactitol.
Why is hepatic fructose metabolism unregulated?
It bypasses PFK-1 (the main glycolytic control point), allowing uncontrolled flux to pyruvate/acetyl-CoA.
